_doc: Events, disasters, festivals and NPC requests (SPEC §18, §19, §21). `rates` are per game year for the whole continent at Knight difficulty; `difficulty` multiplies them (SPEC §1: Squire fewer plagues and famines, King frequent famine, plague and heavy banditry). `calendar` days are the day of the 16-day year. Text pools use {place}, {kingdom}, {name}, {who}, {good}, {qty}, {pence}.

start: The pestilence has come to {place}. The sick are carried out and the church bell tolls all day.
A fever with black swellings strikes {place}; the priest has buried six this week.
Plague in {place}: the market is shut and the gates are watched.
end: The plague has passed from {place}, leaving empty houses and fresh graves.

start: The harvest failed. In {place} the poor are boiling nettles and the price of bread grows.
Hunger in {place}: the granaries are bare and the children cry for bread.
Famine stalks {place}; folk are eating seed corn.
end: The hunger in {place} is over: the new corn is in.

start: Fire in {place}! The thatch is burning and the whole street is out with buckets.
A blaze has broken out in {place}; sparks fly from roof to roof.
{place} is aflame: ring the bell, fetch water!
end: The fire in {place} is out. The neighbours will help to rebuild.

start: The river has burst its banks at {place}; the low houses stand in water.
Floodwater is rising in {place}: folk carry their goods to the church.
end: The waters round {place} are falling; mud and ruin are left behind.

start: No rain has fallen in {kingdom} for weeks. The wells are low and the corn is withering.
A drought grips {kingdom}: the brooks have dried and the ricks are tinder.
end: Rain at last in {kingdom}, too late for much of the corn.

start: A hard winter has set in over {kingdom}. Hungry wolves come down from the hills at night.
Snow lies deep across {kingdom}; the wolves are bold and the poor are cold.
end: The thaw has come in {kingdom}; the wolves go back to the woods.

start: A gang of outlaws has been seen near {place}; folk bar their doors at dusk.
Bandits lurk in the woods by {place}, and the reeve fears for the stores.
The villagers of {place} have refused their dues and gathered with scythes and bills.
Unrest in {place}: the villeins demand an end to the week-work.
{who} is without a grown heir: the great men of {place} whisper of claims and regents.
The succession at {place} is disputed; {who} leaves the title to uncertain hands.
end: The question of the succession at {place} has been settled for now.

start: A tournament is held at {place}: banners, heralds and every young knight in the county.
The yearly fair opens at {place}: merchants from far off, jugglers, and the tolls of three days.
Fair days at {place}! The streets are full of stalls and strangers.
The king's progress has come to {place}; the lord must feed the whole court.
end: The king's court has moved on from {place}.

start: Midsummer eve: bonfires on the hills, garlands on the doors and dancing on the green.
end: The midsummer fires have burnt down.

start: The harvest is in: the last sheaf is carried home with song, and the lord sets the harvest supper.
end: The harvest festival is over; the barns are full.

start: Christmastide: the church is dressed with holly, the lord's hall is open and the Yule log burns.
{name} are wed at the church door of {place}.
{name} is laid to rest in the churchyard of {place}.
{name} is christened at the font of {place}.

ask: I am short of {good}, {name}. Could you bring me {qty}? I will pay you well.
My family has run out of {good}. If you could spare {qty}, I would make it worth your while.
{name}, you are always about. Fetch me {qty} of {good} and there is silver in it for you.
thanks: That will do nicely, {name}. Here is your silver.
God bless you, {name}. We shall not forget this.

ask: I am in a bad way, {name}. Could you lend me {pence}? I will pay it back with interest by the next harvest, on my word.
The reeve has fined me and I cannot pay. Lend me {pence}, {name}, and I shall repay you with a gift on top.
thanks: Bless you. You will have it back, every penny.
I will not forget your kindness, {name}.

ask: My back is bad and the work will not wait. Could you give me {qty} bouts of labour, {name}? I will pay a fair wage.
I need an extra pair of hands for the {qty} jobs that must be done before the weather turns. Will you help?
thanks: Well done, {name}. Here is your wage.

ask: Would you carry a message to {who} at {place}? It is nothing secret, only family business, and I will make it worth the walk.
{name}, I must get word to {who} in {place}, and I have no one to send. Will you go?
thanks: Thank you for bringing it, {name}. That is a weight off my mind.
delivered: So {from} sends word. Thank you for coming all this way; here is something for your trouble.

ask: My {animal} has strayed again, {name}. I think she went towards the {dir}, a few hundred paces out. Would you look for her?
A {animal} of mine is missing since yesterday, somewhere {dir} of the village. I would pay you to find her.
thanks: You found her! God be thanked. Here, take this for your trouble.

ask: Folk are afraid, {name}. Would you stand watch over the village tonight? It would put our minds at rest.
There are strange men in the woods. A sturdy watchman at the green tonight would be a comfort, {name}.
thanks: The village slept sound because of you. Thank you, {name}.

ask: We want to christen the child at the font in two days, and you would honour us by standing godparent, {name}. Will you?
thanks: It was a fine christening. You are family to us now, {name}.

ask: My {relation} {ward} is of an age to wed, and I think highly of you, {name}. Would you wed {ward}? There is a dowry of {pence}.
thanks: Then it is settled. May God bless you both.
